reading.body:
Construction AI is measured, not guessed: Census BTOS surveys firms fortnightly, AGC tracks contractor adoption, and BuiltWorlds plus proptech trackers follow the tools, with computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning as the working deployments.

The pattern is narrow and physical. The named deployments all watch the jobsite or check a digital model against reality before concrete is poured, so the value is in catching discrepancies early, not in generating designs or schedules. That makes construction AI an on-site perception and verification problem, where the binding constraints are accurate site data and timely action before work proceeds.

What the data does not show is how widely these tools are used, what they save, or how often they fail. It establishes that adoption is tracked through a federal survey, a trade body, a research network, and venture flow, but those sources still reflect firms and startups that choose to report, not the entire industry.

summary: Computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning are the working deployments - the sector's AI mostly watches the jobsite and checks the model against reality before concrete is poured.

analysis.body:
The most direct measure of AI use in construction comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Construction (NAICS 23), the latest figure is 17.2%, up from 15.4% in the prior period. The series was first asked in September 2023, and the Census Bureau notes that an S marks suppressed values. This is a firm-reported number rather than an estimate, which makes it the anchor for any claim about how widely the technology has actually spread through the sector.

What the sources describe is a sector where AI is being applied to specific jobsite and preconstruction problems rather than as a general-purpose tool. This page's coverage centers on computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning. BuiltWorlds, which runs the sector intelligence, tracks site robotics, jobsite IoT, and digital preconstruction across research programs and member benchmarking, and its annual AI/ML Conference examines existing and emerging solutions and use cases across the construction, building, and operation process, along with strategies for implementation at the project and enterprise levels and case studies of how companies are using specific solutions. Its Buildings Conference focuses on data centers and AI infrastructure, which points to where some of the demand is coming from as well as where the technology is being deployed.

The trade body record sits with the Associated General Contractors of America, which reports over 27,000 member firms and, per this page, surveys technology adoption and safety-technology compliance across US builders. AGC's data is described here as the adoption record, and its safety programming, including a national event in San Diego for construction safety professionals, connects to the safety-monitoring use case that appears in the coverage. On the money side, CREtech and MetaProp track venture flow across architecture, engineering, and construction technology alongside property tech, which is where the sources place the capital concentration rather than in any single application.

The sources do not report ROI figures for construction AI, and no dollar amounts or payback periods appear in the material. What they do offer on evidence is qualitative: BuiltWorlds describes case studies illustrating how companies are utilizing specific solutions and the lessons learned from their experiences, and a Building Ventures spotlight session at its 2026 AI/ML Conference is framed around founders showcasing AI's practical power in construction. That is the shape of the evidence available here, demonstrations and case studies rather than measured returns.

On risk and regulation, the harvested material is largely silent. No source in the JSON describes construction-specific AI regulation, liability questions, or compliance requirements beyond AGC's mention of safety-technology compliance. A reader should not infer a regulatory posture for the sector from these pages, because none is stated.

For a contractor deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a modest and practical reading. Adoption is real and measured, at 17.2% of firms in the latest Census Bureau reading, and it is concentrated in identifiable applications: safety monitoring by computer vision, clash detection in BIM, and autonomous site scanning. The organizations that track the sector, BuiltWorlds and AGC, are the places to look for benchmarking and adoption data, and the capital trackers CREtech and MetaProp are where the vendor and investment activity is followed. What the sources do not provide is hard ROI evidence, so any business case will have to be built from the reader's own pilot rather than borrowed from these pages.

https://cretech.com/.brief: According to the page, CREtech New York 2026 will be held at the Javits Center in New York City on October 20, 21, 2026, and will bring together 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and more than 20,000 pre-scheduled 1:1 meetings. The event is described as a leading real-estate AI conference where sessions are led by operators actively deploying AI in their portfolios, offering real strategy rather than theory. The conference aims to connect owners, developers, investors, occupiers, construction firms, brokers, and tech leaders to discuss AI’s impact on real-estate assets. Tickets are limited, and sponsors and partners are said to represent companies shaping the future of real-estate in the age of AI.

https://www.agc.org/.brief: The Associated General Contractors of America describes itself as serving more than 27,000 member firms, offering a range of services intended to address members' needs and concerns. According to the organisation, those services aim to improve the quality of construction and to protect the public interest. The page also promotes an event in San Diego that it says brings together construction safety professionals from around the country to share ideas, build relationships, and take proven solutions back to their teams.

https://builtworlds.com/.brief: BuiltWorlds operates a membership network for buildings and infrastructure professionals. The organization hosts an annual Buildings Conference addressing innovation in building development, design, materials and systems, with particular focus on data centers and AI infrastructure. It also runs an annual AI/ML Conference exploring artificial intelligence and machine learning adoption across the architecture, engineering, construction and operations industry, covering implementation strategies, use cases, and lessons learned from companies deploying these technologies.
